newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm price marathon faces grain aid cut block.
newsitem.headline: EU farm price marathon faces grain aid cut block.

text.p: Fierce resistance to proposals to slash aid to cereals farmers risk prolonging the annual European Union farm price marathon starting in Luxembourg on Monday.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler told Reuters this week that he will insist on the need to cut compensatory payments to cereals and oilseed farmers by 1.4 billion ecus to help finance aid for beef producers stricken by the mad cow crisis.
"Yes, I will do it," he said after addressing the European Parliament.
But EU diplomats noted that ministers last year threw out a similar proposal and that all countries, except Britain and Sweden, remained strongly opposed to the move.

"It's hard to see how Fischler can succeed," said one diplomat, adding however that a face-saving formula for Fischler could be a resolution keeping the idea alive by calling for a review of the cut as part of future reforms.

However, Fischler will use a study by the Commission's agriculture directorate showing that cereals farmers were over-paid by 8.5 billion ecus during the past seasons. An earlier British study put the excess at 14.3 billion ecus.
The payments were intended to compensate farmers for cuts in intervention prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms to remove grain, beef and dairy surpluses and to curb costs.
Since then cereals market prices have soared and farmers have been paid for losses they never suffered.
German, French and other farm ministers will argue that it is unfair to make cereals farmers foot the bill for damage caused by bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
They will argue that there is no financial need for the cut, pointing to a recent official estimate showing a 2.0 billion ecus saving in the EU's 1997 farm budget.
A Dutch EU presidency official added that swings in exchange rates meant that the Commission's case for overpayment was not clear-cut.
However, diplomats said blockage of the cereals cuts could harden Fischler's stance against concessions elsewhere.
Ministers will as usual present long shopping lists of sweeteners to the modest package of mainly unchanged prices but a budgetary straightjacket means success will be difficult.
"They increase the price tag, create problems," said a Dutch EU Presidency official.
Apart from cuts in monthly cereals, rice and sugar storage payments and reductions in flax and hemp area aid payments, the Commission has proposed little change.
Demands range from an early fixing of the 1998 cereals set-aside rate, increase in milk quotas, cuts in milk prices and extra aid for sheep, tobacco, olive oil and peas and beans.
Although the Commission will only present a proposal next month for the 1998 set-aside rate, diplomats said that ministers may next week recommend five percent.
"A consensus is growing around an unchanged rate," said one, adding all countries wanted a decision as quickly as possible.
